tasks.title: RED tests for the TUI concurrency defect, silent row dropping, and viewport/legend correctness
tasks.dispositionReason: 18 RED tests across 7 files, all failing on their own assertions; 15 verified by the orchestrator's own run (apps/cli 15 failed / 228 passed) and 3 more added for the ordering half of AC7. D-1's non-event is settled by a causal barrier rather than a timer: a Node parent cannot exit while a child it spawned is alive, so counting the children that announced their argv after the console has closed is exact. Anti-vacuity shown by a throwaway 4-line patch turning the D-1 and D-4 tests green, then reverted with digests re-verified. The contact roster is deliberately left without a pinned ordering, and the reason is right: ContactView carries no time at all, and the roster is a selection surface whose display order cannot be decided apart from the cycle order.

tasks.title: Fix the TUI concurrency defect, row dropping, and viewport/legend correctness
tasks.dispositionReason: All 18 TUI tests green; verified by the orchestrator. The seven test-file digests match T5's record exactly, so the specification was not edited to fit the fix. My first full-suite run showed three extra failures; re-running the affected file in isolation gives 8/8 in 1.7s against 8.9s under load, so those were contention from concurrently running agents driving real processes, not regressions - and the other two belong to the T12 agent's in-progress exploration file. The fix was made at the impure seam rather than in the pure layer: renderFrame was already total at 40x10, and it was runTuiShell.viewport() raising 40 to 72 before calling it. One property was strengthened beyond the brief: the modal's painted-at record is now written only when the viewport was not below the minimum, without which unclamping the width would have made a trust confirmation answerable for identifiers never shown on screen.

tasks.title: Reconcile every document with the tree: stale deletions, the shutdown fix, AC4, and the e2e labelling
tasks.dispositionReason: Documents reconciled with the tree and spot-checked by the orchestrator: the stale clean-shutdown claims are gone from the deployment runbook, and the e2e labelling now names script, files and count in every document that quotes a figure. The agent verified each deletion against the tree itself rather than trusting the inventory, re-ran the four shutdown tests and re-killed the byte-budget mutation in a scratch copy. It also caught the inventory being wrong three times, including one deletion target that would have removed a TRUE statement. Unresolved and carried forward: apps/cli/package.json still runs one of six e2e files (T9's scope), there is no root test:e2e so the gate command cannot run as written, the renewal timer is still not installed on depr, and geekom's CertDomains was not re-checked after the toggle.

tasks.title: RED tests for the relay FIX NOW items: cleanup timer, backfill skip-and-count, poll byte budget, v1 identifier bounds, shutdown escalation
tasks.dispositionReason: 9 Go tests across 6 new files; RED confirmed by the orchestrator's own run: cleanup Stop, relay stops cleanup before closing storage, backfill skip-and-count (2 tests), pre-binding authorization, poll byte budget, and the identifier bounds, with a green control that the bound does not close the route. RI-31's two escalation paths could not be RED because they are untested rather than wrong; the agent proved non-vacuity instead by three out-of-tree mutations of main.go, each killed by exactly one new test and by none of the four pre-existing ones. It also caught two of its own tests passing vacuously because t.TempDir() puts the test name into the logged data-dir path, and narrowed both. Two findings raised: RI-19 was wrong in both directions (device_id accepted and stored unbounded, never a 500; identity_id already refused incidentally), and RI-09 is a two-sided change rather than relay-internal.

tasks.title: Implement the relay FIX NOW items
tasks.dispositionReason: Four items implemented; re-verified by the orchestrator under -race -tags relayv2: exactly one failure, the RI-09 test that was deliberately left red, every other package ok, 0 data races. All six test-file digests unchanged from T8. The cleanup service is now stopped between the drain and the Badger close, its Stop() joins the goroutine rather than only signalling it, and all four post-router storage-close paths go through the same helper. NewRouter keeps a single return value with chi.Mux embedded rather than the two-value shape the tests-creator's throwaway patch used, because that shape would have broken four existing call sites the implementer may not edit.

tasks.title: RED tests for the two-sided max-message-size derivation (RI-09)
tasks.dispositionReason: Two client-side RED tests plus an analysis that located every limit. Established: the relay's maximum is per-deployment and unbounded above, never checked by Config.Validate(); the client's is a compiled-in literal unreachable from configuration, and the client applies NO send-side bound at all, so it will post a ciphertext it then refuses to read back; a shared protocol constant already exists and is used nowhere, with the same value hand-written in four places, so consuming it removes duplication rather than adding coupling; and the relay advertises no maximum on any route. Neither test can be passed by moving a literal: one asserts only that the client's two size opinions agree, the other that one max-size envelope is accepted AND eight are still refused. The agent also warned that the frozen Go test compares against a mirror constant the implementer may edit, which is the likeliest false green here.

tasks.title: Implement the two-sided max-message-size derivation (RI-09)
tasks.dispositionReason: Both client tests green, the Go test deliberately still red, and the agent proved by measurement that no product-code change can close both: clamping the handler's maximum makes the frozen acceptance test fail with 413 where it wants 200, so exactly one can be green and the frozen one wins. It did NOT edit the mirror constant, both because it lives in a test file and because doing so would assert an acceptance that does not exist - the false green I warned about. The protocol constant now has consumers on both sides; hand-written copies went from four to two. apps/cli 255/255, typecheck 0, Go untagged and both race configurations each with only that one failure and 0 data races. Operational check by the orchestrator: both live relays set the variable to exactly the protocol maximum, so neither would be refused at its next restart.

tasks.title: RED test: a failed mailbox deposit must not permanently consume the recipient's one-time prekey bundle
tasks.dispositionReason: Three RED client-side tests, and an analysis that REFUTED the orchestrator's framing of the finding. Established by measurement: the claim and the deposit are two separate client-issued requests with no shared transaction; the T11 failure was server-side on the second request (403 UNAUTHORIZED_MAILBOX_ACCESS, because the sender had never run relay publish); the same-sender retry is already correct, running off the durable outbox and reusing an identical claim_id, and the T11 retry failed only because it came from a fresh profile, i.e. a genuinely different sender; and relay-side replenishment already works end to end against real Badger. The claim is legitimately permanent - a rollback would hand one Signal one-time prekey to two senders, and the relay cannot know the deposit failed because the sender may still deliver from its durable outbox. The agent therefore added no Go test and touched none of the three existing guards. What remains are two client-side bounds and one genuine security finding.

tasks.title: Fix the unrolled-back prekey claim, or bound it explicitly
tasks.dispositionReason: Two of three green; the third is not implementable without a decision above the task, and the agent proved that rather than asserting it: it implemented the guard predicate, measured 36 failures across nine files including an e2e test that pins the current behaviour against the real relay binary, reverted fully and edited no test. Test file digest unchanged. apps/cli 248 passed / 1 failed of 249 across 44 files including the real-relay e2e suites. A dead stored claim is now recovered by one retry, with a fresh claim id written durably BEFORE the second claim - the same ordering that made the first recoverable - and the caller sees claimReplaced: true, absent on every ordinary send. A pin failure is still CONTACT_PIN_MISMATCH; an expired bundle is no longer mislabelled as one.

tasks.title: Install certificate renewal on depr, matching geekom
tasks.dispositionReason: Renewal is automated on both hosts; verified by the orchestrator directly: geekom's user-scope timer and depr's root-scope timer both report enabled and active, and both relays answer 200 over HTTPS with ssl_verify_result=0. depr was deliberately NOT converted to geekom's volume arrangement: that would mean replacing a running container today to make two hosts look alike, against an expiry nine months out, and the volume route exists only to work around a privilege depr already has. The repository's committed systemd units were used byte-for-byte on depr, so the artifact is now proven somewhere rather than dead code everywhere. Delivery to the running container was proven positively rather than by a tautological digest comparison: the agent perturbed the PUBLIC cert file to a strictly more restrictive mode, confirmed the container saw it, ran the unit, and confirmed the container saw the restoration - a state only the unit could produce. The private key was never touched and never world-readable.

tasks.title: Correct deploy/relay/README.md: the committed systemd units are root-and-host-path only
tasks.dispositionReason: The README row now states that the committed units assume a root install and host paths, that a host without usable root renews by a different user-scope mechanism with the same schedule and no-restart contract, and that the status command differs - which is the silent trap, since checking with the wrong scope reports nothing rather than erroring. It cross-references the runbook rather than duplicating its comparison.

tasks.title: Record that the process-spawning CLI tests fail under CPU contention and decide whether to harden or serialise them
tasks.dispositionReason: Cause found and measured rather than guessed: five suites each hard-coded their own per-child kill watchdog sized for an idle machine, a second timeout layer that was never updated when the enclosing one was raised once before on the same evidence. Port collisions, shared temp directories and worker-pool misconfiguration were ruled out. Reproduced twice, then measured under 70-way core oversubscription: the heaviest command needs 19.7 to 20.4 s against a 15 s wall. Before the fix 9 of 36 failed at that load, after it 36 of 36 passed. The five drifting literals became one shared documented module; idle wall-clock is unchanged because these are ceilings rather than delays.

tasks.title: Add a CLI entry point for bundle rotation so a consumed bundle is recoverable
tasks.dispositionReason: Superseded by the T18 design's recommended companion. A pool of N published one-time bundles raises the attacker's price linearly - 120/N victims per minute against 120 - and gives the victim recovery through relay publish, a command that already exists. That needs a changed meaning for an existing command rather than a ninth one, which is strictly better for a deliberately frozen eight-command surface. Reopen only if replenishment turns out not to deliver recovery.

tasks.title: Design: authenticate /v2/prekeys/claim to close the denial-of-first-contact primitive
tasks.dispositionReason: Design delivered with the hole reproduced end to end against the real relay binary: a stranger's raw claim, no key material and no publication, only the victim's public identity id, answers 200 with a bundle in 5 ms; the victim's republish then reports claimable false and a genuine published sender is refused. The honest headline is that authentication does NOT raise the attacker's cost - it adds a step. Measured: setup goes from nothing to 2.9 ms and one unauthenticated POST, and victims per minute from one source go from 120 to 119 in the first minute and 120 thereafter, because identities mint at 349 per second. What it buys is stated as capability rather than cost: the keyless-attacker class disappears, consumption becomes attributable, and every non-CLI caller is covered - the reproduction was a raw fetch, so the client-side guard that landed earlier is a courtesy and not a control. Alternatives were rejected with measurements rather than preferences, and one was explicitly NOT rejected.

tasks.title: RED tests: send must refuse before claiming when the sender has not published
tasks.dispositionReason: Four new RED tests plus a strengthened e2e case, and eleven fixture files corrected without weakening any. Every new test asserts on the requests actually issued and on the durable store keys, not only on the thrown error, because the load-bearing property is that the network call never happens. The e2e case was moved earlier so the real relay binary witnesses that the recipient's bundle survives an unpublished sender's attempt: the old form could only observe what the sender was told, the new form observes what the sender cost a third party, and the original PREKEY assertions were kept verbatim as a later step issued by a published sender. Achievability proved with a throwaway probe that first reproduced T13's exact 36-failure damage and then went fully green after the corrections, reverted with both product files hashing to baseline.

tasks.title: Implement: send presupposes relay publish
tasks.dispositionReason: Landed in commit e949aae; the send precondition is implemented and its tests are green.

tasks.title: Re-author the poll-budget test: pin deliverability at the protocol maximum, not at a refused configuration
tasks.dispositionReason: Re-authored in place; the file and its RI-09 provenance stay, the test NAME is retired because it named exactly the premise the design decision invalidated, and both files carry the retired name in their headers so the history reads from the code. One red test became five green tests over ten sub-cases, and nothing was dropped: the replacement removes the old permissive or-refused branch, keeps the bound and delivery assertions, adds a stored-count assertion, and runs at three configurations instead of one. Every case first passes its maximum through the real Validate(), so the test cannot drift back into asserting a relay that does not start. No size is a literal anywhere, and non-vacuity was proved by two out-of-tree mutations: widening the derived bound fails the guard, and doubling the protocol constant leaves deliverability green while three other assertions fail by name - so the tests track the relationship rather than the number. The mirror constant was not touched; instead it is now a checked derivation in place, because it already equals the client's rule. Verified by the orchestrator: go test -race -tags relayv2 exit 0, nine packages ok, 0 data races.

tasks.title: Refuse a zero maximum message size, and correct the fixtures that build a zero-value config
tasks.dispositionReason: Verified by the orchestrator: go test -race -count=1 -tags relayv2 exit 0, ten packages ok, 0 data races. The agent found the distinction I had not made in the brief: a zero-value struct is an idiomatic Go default and Validate() cannot tell it apart from an explicitly set 0, so refusing there would outlaw the struct default in order to reach the operator - the wrong end. It resolved the zero once in the handler so the two consumers that disagreed are handed the same number by construction, and put the loud refusal in Load(), the only place that can distinguish set-to-zero from unset. It also measured the six fixtures rather than repeating the claim, and noted that six understates it because two more callers stay green only by requiring any error. Two router fixtures were corrected, and that is a strengthening: they were working around a panic this task removed and pinned closed.

tasks.title: The push-gate fix lives in untracked .git/hooks and keryx update will revert it; make it durable
tasks.dispositionReason: Gate hardened and PROVED: pnpm run gate:selftest reports 27 ok, 0 wrong, 0 skipped, re-run by the orchestrator. The interrupted work's own claim that the gate was tracked and would survive a clone was FALSE - it was untracked, so a clone would have received no gate at all, exactly the failure being fixed. Moving to core.hooksPath also opened a cheaper silent revert, since one local config unset falls back to the stock hook that allows a push having run nothing; closed by a tripwire in the only file git can still reach, which announces the gate is missing AND execs the tracked gate anyway. Cost measured: +27 s, +12 percent, with the Go relay suite going from never running to 26 s race-enabled; no subset taken because -race costs 3 s and the relay's guarantees are concurrency guarantees. Freshness warns on drift and blocks on a broken pin - a check that fails every ordinary push gets disabled within a day, and deleting the pin line is otherwise the cheapest way to switch it off invisibly.

tasks.title: RED tests for bundle replenishment: a pool of N, top-up through relay publish
tasks.dispositionReason: Thirteen tests across five groups, with the two Go tests honestly labelled as green regression pins rather than dressed up as red, because the tree already satisfies them and nothing had asserted them. The load-bearing negative is pinned: refilling never prunes or re-uses allocated key material. The authorised e2e rewrite kept steps 1-5 byte-identical, replaced a boolean that a pool makes false with exact counts, and MOVED the exhausted-prekey assertions intact behind a full drain performed by raw unauthenticated claims - the attack itself - rather than deleting them. Two findings the design missed: six existing assertions counting publish requests, and a relay error code that the transport discards so a test could not have passed without adding it.

tasks.title: Correct the six publish-count assertions that become false at N=20, without loosening them
tasks.dispositionReason: Six assertions corrected to the new exact truth, none loosened. The agent found that two of them needed more than an arithmetic change: at index 1 the array under a pool holds an unrelated slot from the FIRST call rather than the second call's resubmission, so fixing only the length would have silently broken what the assertion pins; and the rotation test's negative-index reads would have passed for the wrong reason or thrown a raw type error instead of a clean assertion. N is derived from the protocol constant rather than written as 20. Suite went from 13 red to 19 red, exactly six more, each a clean assertion failure with no type error and no timeout.

tasks.title: Implement bundle replenishment: a pool of N with top-up through relay publish
tasks.dispositionReason: Pool implemented in product code only, four files, 18 of 19 target tests passing including the real-relay e2e: 20 senders delivered from one pool, 20 decrypted in one poll, the 21st refused at exit 3, one relay publish restored the pool and the refused sender's own retry then delivered. Slot 0 keeps its key, schema and bytes so the send precondition does not regress. Empty slots fill highest-index-down so slot 0 carries the youngest timestamp and stays the stable anchor while being the last member a claim reaches. The nineteenth failure is a defect in the test rather than the implementation - it contradicts step 6 of its own file - and the implementer correctly refused to edit a test to make its own work pass. It also found a second publish-counting site that both earlier passes missed, because that one counts through a filter rather than an assertion.

tasks.title: Correct two test defects the pool exposed: a self-contradicting drain count and a filtered publish count
tasks.dispositionReason: Both corrections applied after the agent CONFIRMED the diagnosis rather than applying it: it traced the pool state by hand across the file and cross-checked against a second test that fixes what pool.claimable means, which is what rules out the rejected reading - that reading would have falsified the other test instead. Counts derive from the protocol constant, not literals. Its search for the missed class found the four filter-based counting sites in the two-process file and filter closures in five more files, and established that only one referenced the publish route. One failure remains and is a different class, correctly left alone and reported.

tasks.title: Fix the inbound store-snapshot test the pool's mint-before-offer design invalidated
tasks.dispositionReason: The assertion's property was established and preserved rather than rebased to a new number. It is an atomicity pin - a persistence failure inside send()'s own commit must roll back exactly what that transaction wrote - and NOT a claim that send() as a whole leaves the store untouched. The old form worked only because the pool had one member, which was an artefact of size rather than the invariant. The fix adds an optional hook to the shared test helper that captures the baseline after publish and before send; the other ten call sites pass nothing and are unchanged. The comparison is now before-and-after within the test, encoding no count anywhere, so it survives any future pool size. Non-vacuity checked: at the capture point the pool is full and the other store sections are empty, so a leaked partial rollback still fails it.
